source.title_on_document: When ChatGPT is gone: Creativity reverts and homogeneity persists

paper_design_summary: Sixty-one college students were randomly assigned to use ChatGPT 4.0 (n = 31) or to work alone (n = 30) in a seven-day lab experiment. Each day they did an alternative uses test (AUT) and a product-feature problem-solving task; Day 1 and Day 7 were done without ChatGPT by everyone, ChatGPT was available to the treatment group on Days 2 to 6, and a one-month follow-up AUT (Day 30) was done without ChatGPT. Blind raters scored AUT novelty, usefulness, and flexibility and the problem-solving answers for creativity and value, and SBERT cosine similarity and string matching measured homogeneity of responses within each group.

studies.label: Seven-day lab experiment with Day 30 follow-up (AUT and product problem-solving)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Use of ChatGPT 4.0 on the creative tasks of Days 2 to 6 versus completing the same tasks alone
assignment.quote: After consenting to the study, they were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: ChatGPT use (the treatment group, n = 31) and no ChatGPT use (the control group, n = 30).

arms.name: ChatGPT use (treatment / 'GPT' / 'Experimental' / Group E)
arms.description: Given ChatGPT 4.0 to help finish the two creative tasks on Days 2 to 6; no ChatGPT on Day 1, Day 7, and Day 30

arms.name: No ChatGPT use (control / Group C)
arms.description: Completed the same two creative tasks by themselves on all days

participants.exclusions: None reported. Section 2.1 describes the 61 as students who 'completed the lab experiment'; Table 1 note says N=61. Per-arm analyzed counts are not printed separately (31 + 30 = 61). The number of people who did the Day 30 follow-up is not stated.
participants.who: College students with 31 different majors (undergraduates, graduates, and Ph.D. candidates); mean age 21.56 (SD 2.62); 36 female
participants.quote: Sixty-one college students (Mage = 21.56 years, SD = 2.62) with 31 different majors from a university completed the lab experiment (per-registered at https://osf.io/hea8r). 36 of them were female.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 24, Section 4.2 (undergraduates, graduates, Ph.D. candidates)

ai_tool.how_used: Treatment participants were provided ChatGPT 4.0 'to help them to finish the creative tasks' on Days 2 to 6 (p. 5). The paper does not describe prompts, instructions, or limits on use.

task.description: Two tasks each day in counterbalanced order: (1) a low-complexity AUT listing creative uses for an everyday object (e.g., pen, brick; Day 30 used a sponge); (2) a high-complexity problem-solving task proposing new functions or solutions for a company's product (e.g., VR glasses). Task 2 is closer to idea_generation. The paper gives the number of tasks inconsistently: 16 (p. 3), 14 (p. 4), and 8 AUT plus 7 product tasks (p. 24).
task.duration: AUT: at most 3 minutes; Task 2: no time limit. Seven consecutive days plus a follow-up one month later.

outcomes.name: AUT novelty (Days 2 to 6, ChatGPT available)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two blind raters (consensual assessment technique) scored each AUT idea for novelty; participant novelty = sum of idea scores, so it also rises with the number of ideas. ICCs >= .90. Raters' background not stated. Welch/Student t-tests (R broom/dplyr) by day.

outcomes.question: with_ai

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity of AUT responses within group (Days 2 to 6, ChatGPT available)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: SBERT cosine similarity (higher = more homogeneous; sign reversed for diversity). Variants reported for the same outputs: string-matching 'redundancy' (shared character sequences longer than two characters; lexical_overlap) in Table 3, and dispersion of PCA(30) then UMAP(2) projections of SBERT embeddings (standard deviation, sum of eigenvalues, ellipse area) in Table 4a, with no tests.

String matching Control vs GPT: Day 2 2.73 vs 5.9; Day 3 3.17 vs 8.24; Day 4 3.33 vs 7.12; Day 5 3.4 vs 8.73; Day 6 3.13 vs 7.95; text 'MC = [3.13, 3.4], ME = [5.90, 8.73], ps <= .01'. Table 4a SD Control vs GPT: D2 0.40 vs 0.33; D3 0.34 vs 0.41; D4 0.37 vs 0.32; D5 0.36 vs 0.33; D6 0.37 vs 0.32.

diversity_detail.metric: Mean SBERT cosine similarity between responses within a group (Table 3 'SBERT'); string-matching redundancy as cross-validation
diversity_detail.embedding_model: SBERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019); the paper says 'we first trained the SBERT model' and names no checkpoint
diversity_detail.computed_over: Cosine similarity between pairs of responses ('S1' and 'S2'); the paper does not say which pairs are compared (e.g., all pairs within a condition) or whether the unit is an idea or a participant's full response
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Not described; the text gives 'ps <= .01' for Days 2 to 6 without naming the test. Table 3 note says unbolded numbers are significant at p <= .001, but no cell is bolded.
diversity_detail.notes: The text's ME range '[0.35, 59]' does not match Table 3 (GPT Days 2 to 6 range 0.45 to 0.59). Dispersion measures (Table 4a) mostly but not always point the same way (Day 3 SD 0.34 vs 0.41).

company_involvement.description: Co-author Jihao Huang is affiliated with Beijing Yuxin Technology Company; the paper states no role for the company and no AI-company funding or involvement.

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to ChatGPT 4.0 versus no AI on AUT and product problem-solving tasks (p. 4, Section 2.1); 61 people analyzed (31 + 30; Table 1 note N=61), above 50 but not by much; outcomes are blind-rated novelty, usefulness, and creativity of outputs plus SBERT similarity across participants (pp. 6, 13-16). The Day 30 follow-up sample size is not stated.

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT on Days 2 to 6, users scored higher on AUT novelty (Day 6: 39.84 vs 14.80, t = -4.84, p = 0.000; p. 8 Table 2a, p. 11 Table 1) and Task 2 creativity, but not on Day 7 without AI (novelty 17.60 vs 13.02, p = 0.053), while their AUT responses stayed more similar at Day 30 (SBERT 0.39 vs 0.33, p <= .001; p. 14, p. 16 Table 3).
open_questions: Day 30 AUT novelty: Table 1 gives Estimate -3.69, P 0.038 (significant), but Table 2a means are 2.40 vs 2.56 and the text (p. 7) says no significant difference. Which is correct?
Day 30 AUT usefulness: Table 1 Estimate -6.26 does not equal the Table 2a mean difference (5.62 vs 5.55).
Day 7 Task 2 usefulness is significant in Table 1 and Figure 2b (P = 0.021), but the text says all Day 7 p-values were insignificant.
Task 2 'usefulness' appears in Table 1 and Figure 2b but not among the four ratings described in Section 2.3 or in Table 2b.

Tables 2a, 2b, and 3 notes say unbolded numbers are significant at p <= .001, which conflicts with Table 1 p-values (e.g., Day 2 AUT novelty p = 0.031; Day 4 Task 2 creativity p = 0.055) and with no bolding in Tables 2a and 3.
Table 2a Day 1 novelty means (7.50 vs 8.78) look lower than the Day 1 bars in Figure 2a (about 15 and 17).
The text's string-matching Day 1 values (0.36 vs 0.35, p. 15) repeat the SBERT values; Table 3 gives 3.44 vs 3.51.
Which pairs of responses enter the SBERT similarity and what test produced 'ps <= .01' and 'p <= .001' are not stated.
Number of participants who completed the Day 30 follow-up is not stated.
The preregistration (osf.io/hea8r) is not described in the paper; primary outcomes are not named.
notes: Single study with repeated daily outcomes. I listed 15 outcomes and left out the AUT recognition accuracy measures (Judgement N and Judgement U: the gap between a participant's self-selected best idea and their top-scored idea; Table 1, Table 2a, appendix Figure 2a p. 28), which are not creativity ratings of the output; mostly ns with isolated significant days. I grouped Task 2 content quality, public favor, and market success into S1-O6 (and with usefulness into S1-O13 for Day 7) and folded string matching and UMAP dispersion into the SBERT outcomes as variants. Table 1 'Estimate' is Control minus GPT (Day 2 AUT novelty: 30.77 - 41.55 = -10.78), so negative values mean the GPT arm scored higher. Tests are t-tests by day at the participant level (p. 7); no SDs or SEs are printed. AUT scores are sums over ideas, so novelty and usefulness also reflect fluency. The dataset holds 3302 AUT ideas and 427 Task 2 solutions (p. 1); AUT ideas per day ranged from 351 (Day 7) to 501 (Day 4), 5.75 per person on average (p. 5). Task type is set to divergent_test for the study, but Task 2 is a product idea-generation task. Day 1 (pre-treatment, no AI) is a baseline and not coded as an outcome.
